record.file_problem: The full paper is present. Some extracted tables and figures are flattened or have imperfect formatting.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports downstream benchmark performance across model sizes, which bears on downstream scaling, but it does not measure or fit held-out pretraining loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites prior scaling-law work and says revised scaling laws motivated training larger models for an additional 25 billion tokens on repeated data. That is a design choice, not a test of the laws. It reports no held-out pretraining cross-entropy sweep, small-run loss extrapolation, or compute-optimal allocation sweep. Rows record its own downstream results across model sizes; cited scaling results are not rows.
record.test_reason: The paper evaluates its own BLOOM/BLOOMZ size series (560M–176B) on downstream tasks. These results bear on whether downstream performance improves with scale in a new multilingual setting (V6). It reports no pretraining-loss curves, extrapolation, compute-optimal sweeps or architecture-shape comparisons, and fits no predictive law.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude BLOOM is competitive and improves after multitask finetuning. On scale, they say summarization and code performance increase with model size, while SuperGLUE gains with scale are very slight. They make no claims about loss scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: This paper reports downstream benchmark performance across model sizes rather than fitting held-out pretraining loss curves, extrapolating loss, or estimating compute-optimal parameter/token allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: SuperGLUE results vary by task and prompt; the authors report only slight and inconsistent gains from zero-shot to one-shot and that only models above 2 billion parameters show scale-related signal. WikiLingua results are per-prompt and per-language.

fits_no_version.finding: Multilingual probing: BLOOM-1B7 scores on par with or better than BLOOM-176B on morphosyntactic probing (Mann-Whitney p<0.01, Table 13), though the larger model is more stable across languages.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linguistic information linearly decodable from representations does not increase with model scale.

record.problems: The scale-related downstream evidence is limited: SuperGLUE gains are described as slight, only some sizes show signal, and WikiLingua scores are figure-only. The paper does not fit a predictive scaling relation or report uncertainty for the scale-series benchmark results.
record.rows_left_out: Did not add rows for other evaluations that do not compare downstream results across scale or otherwise test V6, including translation, HELM, embedding, probing, and bias results. Cited scaling-law findings and design decisions based on them are not the paper's own scaling-law test results.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss reported or fitted against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fixed-compute allocation analysis. Training extra tokens after Hoffmann et al. is a design choice, not a test.
Shape ablations are referenced to Le Scao et al. (2022), not reported here as loss comparisons.
No power-law fits in other modalities or regimes.
Predictability is untested: no functional fit, no forecast of larger models from smaller ones, and no relation of downstream score to pretraining loss.
No analysis of fitting choices or curve bending.

missing.what: Per-task, per-prompt one-shot SuperGLUE accuracies across BLOOM and OPT sizes, which would show where the flat region ends
Per-language WikiLingua ROUGE-2 scores by BLOOM size

record.verdict_notes: BLOOM is a model-release paper. Its scaling evidence consists only of monotonic downstream improvement across six sizes, with no fitted relation, so it cannot test the 'predictably' part of V6. HumanEval BLOOMZ-176B underperforms BLOOM-176B, but that compares finetuning effects, not scale.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No test of predicting much larger runs’ loss from fits to smaller runs.
No fixed-compute comparison or fitted parameter/token allocation trend.
No reported fixed-parameter loss comparison varying depth, width, or other architecture details in this paper.
No test of power-law loss forms across other modalities or training regimes; using repeated data for some training does not itself test this.

Tests downstream performance across scale on HumanEval and reports qualitative scaling results for SuperGLUE and WikiLingua. Does not test downstream performance against pretraining loss or fit a quantitative predictive law.
No analysis of how loss-law exponents or compute-optimal splits vary with fitting choices, or whether loss curves bend from a power law.

rows.subject: BLOOM-560M
rows.operation_detail: HumanEval code-generation benchmark, varying model size
rows.note: One of the reported pretrained BLOOM model sizes; the table reports separate pass@k measures.
rows.check: Each row is one point of a size series; marking every point 'partial' is wrong. Read as a series, all three pass@k measures rise monotonically from 560M to 176B (pass@1 0.82%→15.52%, pass@100 5.91%→55.45%). R01, the smallest model, is effectively the baseline. No fitted law is reported.

rows.subject: BLOOM models (size series)
rows.operation_detail: Compared one-shot SuperGLUE performance across BLOOM and OPT model sizes

conditions.value: one-shot; average accuracy across five prompts per task

rows.value: Both BLOOM and OPT improve very slightly with scale; only models over 2 billion parameters show signal.
rows.note: The prose reports this family-level result; Figure 8 displays per-task prompt results but does not provide tabulated values.
